Korea Entry Forms

Before you fly

5 slides · 1080×1350 (4:5) · @goodlugg · R2_KoreaEntryFormsWhatToSortBeforeYouLand/

Scroll the strip sideways, the way the carousel swipes

Caption

Here's what nobody tells you about landing in Korea right now: the form you've been stressing over is probably not the one you need. Twenty-two nationalities are exempt from the K-ETA through 31 December 2026 — Japan, Taiwan, Hong Kong, Macao, Singapore, the US, Canada, the UK, Australia, New Zealand, plus twelve European countries (not all of Europe, so check the list). Exempt means you board without one. The form that actually catches people is the e-Arrival Card. It's free, it opens three days before you land, and the only place to do it is e-arrivalcard.go.kr. Korea Immigration put out a warning in March about fake sites charging for it, in six languages, which tells you how common that got. One quirk worth knowing: hold an approved K-ETA and you skip the arrival card entirely. That's the trade — you pay the government fee, you file nothing at the border. Ten minutes on the sofa now, nothing to do at the airport later. Then hand us the bags and go start the trip. Apps You Actually Need

Before you fly

5 slides · 1080×1350 (4:5) · @goodlugg · R1_AppsYouActuallyNeedInKorea/

Scroll the strip sideways, the way the carousel swipes

Caption

Everyone tells you Korea runs on apps. Nobody tells you that the apps you already have mostly won't work — and it isn't the language. Every big Korean app has an English mode now. The wall is identity: most of them want a Korean phone number registered in your name, which you won't have. So Korea grew a second tier of apps built for visitors. k.ride instead of Kakao T — sign up with an email, pay the driver in the cab. WOWPASS instead of a Korean bank card — load it with cash at a kiosk. Naver added passport login in June, so you can book a restaurant without a local number. And download KakaoTalk before you land: your hotel, your host and your driver will all message you there, not by SMS. The odd one out is Google Maps. It can't route you for driving or walking here — a Korean mapping law keeps the high-precision data inside the country. Naver Map does it in English, exit numbers and all. Save this for the trip. Where a Foreign Card Fails

Save-worthy

5 slides · 1080×1350 (4:5) · @goodlugg · R3_WhereAForeignCardFailsInKorea/

Scroll the strip sideways, the way the carousel swipes

Caption

Korea reads as fully cashless until you try to pay for the thing that actually moves you. Your Visa is fine at the hotel and the department store. It's transit machines, the self-order kiosks in cafés and fast food, and market stalls that stop you dead. The fix is one card, bought on day one. T-money is sold at GS25, CU, 7-ELEVEN and subway stations, and it pays for taxis and convenience stores as well as trains. Reloads at a store counter are cash, so keep small notes on you. Prefer to load foreign cash? WOWPASS kiosks do that with your passport, and the card taps as T-money. New since 17 March 2026: 440 ticket machines across 273 Seoul stations take foreign Visa and Mastercard for single-journey tickets and Climate Card passes, at an average 3.7% fee. The gates themselves still won't read your card. Seoul is aiming at 2030 for that. Save this before you land. And if you'd rather not wrestle a kiosk with a suitcase against your leg, we'll move your bags across Korea the same day. Korea Without a Car

Save-worthy

5 slides · 1080×1350 (4:5) · @goodlugg · R4_KoreaWithoutACar/

Scroll the strip sideways, the way the carousel swipes

Caption

Korea's intercity network is superb at moving people. It's completely indifferent to your suitcase. There's no baggage car on any KTX. Korail's own rule: you carry your bags yourself, two pieces maximum, nothing on a seat, nothing in the aisle. That's the entire policy. So the real question when you plan Seoul to Busan isn't which train you take. It's what happens to the suitcase you're hauling up the platform. Worth saving for the trip: Korail sells tickets and shows schedules only one month ahead, so the good slots go early. On one live search for a Monday in August, 8 of the 10 evening KTX departures were already sold out in economy. Buses split into express (expressway, no stops in between) and intercity (more stops, smaller towns), and neither has a toilet on board — you stop at highway service areas instead. And if you'd rather travel with your hands free, that part's ours. We take the bags city to city while you take the fast train. First-Timer Mistakes

Save-worthy

5 slides · 1080×1350 (4:5) · @goodlugg · R9_KoreaFirstTimerMistakes/

Scroll the strip sideways, the way the carousel swipes

Caption

First-timers spend weeks worrying about bowing angles and then get stopped cold by a bus door. Here's the honest order of operations. Download Naver Map or Kakao Map before you land — Korea's own tourism board tells you to, because Korean law restricts the detailed map data Google needs, and turn-by-turn still isn't there. Get a T-money card before your first bus, because buses in Incheon, Daegu and Gwangju don't take cash at all and plenty of Seoul buses have followed. Tap on and tap off, every ride, or the free transfer never happens. And if you buy the Seoul Climate Card, know what it isn't: it doesn't cover airport buses, the Sinbundang Line, or Incheon and Gyeonggi buses. Stuck anywhere? 1330 is a free travel helpline with English on the line, from anywhere in the country. Save this one for week one. Then swipe to the last slide — doing all of that with two suitcases is its own separate problem, and that part we handle. 23 kg vs 32 kg

Good luggage

5 slides · 1080×1350 (4:5) · @goodlugg · R5_23KgVs32KgAirlineBaggageRulesIntoKorea/

Scroll the strip sideways, the way the carousel swipes

Caption

Two different problems, and people mix them up constantly. Being over your allowance is a conversation at the desk. Being over 32 kg in one bag is a wall. Asiana puts it plainly: for the safety of the baggage handlers, a checked bag shouldn't exceed 32 kg — and above that, carriage may be denied. That limit exists to protect the people lifting your bag onto the belt, which is why no amount of money moves it. You repack on the terminal floor instead. Two more that catch travellers out. Asiana won't check a bag at the gate, duty-free included — so whatever you buy airside comes into the cabin with you. And since 26 January 2026, Korean Air, Asiana, Jin Air, Air Busan and Air Seoul don't let you use or charge a power bank in flight. Keep it within arm's reach, tape over the metal ports or put each one in its own pouch. The counters hand out the tape. Save this for the night before you fly. Cabin-only vs Cabin-banned

Good luggage

5 slides · 1080×1350 (4:5) · @goodlugg · R6_CabinonlyVsCabinbanned/

Scroll the strip sideways, the way the carousel swipes

Caption

Here's the sorting rule that makes packing decisions instant: a delivered bag is a checked bag that left early. So the question was never valuable vs cheap. It's cabin-only vs cabin-banned. Cabin-only stays on you. Power banks and spare batteries are banned from checked baggage outright. Cash, cards and cheques, Korean couriers can refuse to carry at all. Your passport and anything irreplaceable on paper belongs in your pocket anyway. Cabin-banned is what the bag is for. The full-size toner, the aerosol sunscreen, the 300ml of everything that turns airport security into a small tragedy. A bag travelling by road doesn't care about the 100ml rule. And the one line almost nobody fills in: the declared value. Under Korea's standard courier terms, leave it blank and compensation is capped at a flat ceiling no matter what was inside. Write the value in and it's calculated on what you declared instead. Save this one for the trip. Then go see Korea with your hands free. Korea's Autumn, Back to Front

Travel news

5 slides · 1080×1350 (4:5) · @goodlugg · R7_KoreasAutumnBackToFront/

Scroll the strip sideways, the way the carousel swipes

Caption

Korea's autumn has two halves, and most trip plans get them the wrong way round. The crowds come first. Chuseok runs 24–27 September, a four-day break with the whole country on the move. Then two long weekends back to back: 3–5 October for National Foundation Day, 9–11 October for Hangeul Day. Korea Herald points out the second week of October is a three-day working week. The colour comes last. Across 414 mountains the average peak lands around 26 October, and it keeps drifting later — Surisan hit peak on 31 October in 2025, nearly two weeks later than a decade earlier. Down south, the colour holds into November. Which means the quiet weeks and the pretty weeks are the same weeks. Go mid-October onward and you still catch Busan's film festival (6–15 Oct), Jinju's lantern festival on the Namgang (3–18 Oct), Yeosu's island exhibition until 4 November, and fireworks over Gwangalli on 7 November. Move light between all of it. We'll take the bags. Three Days in Busan

Travel plan

5 slides · 1080×1350 (4:5) · @goodlugg · R8_ThreeDaysInBusanBagsIncluded/

Scroll the strip sideways, the way the carousel swipes

Caption

Busan's first day is usually Gamcheon Culture Village. Here's the part nobody puts in the itinerary: the only public way up is a village minibus from Toseong Station Exit 6 — Saha 1-1, Seogu 2 or Seogu 2-2 — and Busan's own tourism site publishes a city bus luggage limit of 20 kg, nothing bigger than 50×40×20 cm. That's roughly a 20-inch carry-on. A checked suitcase doesn't fit the rule. The usual fallback is a coin locker, and the numbers are thinner than you'd think. Toseong has 7 extra-large lockers in the entire station. Haeundae has 154 lockers but only 29 extra-large. Gwangan, for Gwangalli Beach, has 10. Nampo and Jagalchi are the exception — 56 and 45 extra-large, right by the B1 ticket gates. So build Day 1 around the old town, keep Haeundae and the Sky Capsule for Day 2, and save the north end of Line 1 for Day 3. Or hand us the bags and stop counting lockers altogether. Long Layover, Seoul

Travel plan

5 slides · 1080×1350 (4:5) · @goodlugg · R10_LongLayoverSeoul/

Scroll the strip sideways, the way the carousel swipes

Caption

Long layover at Incheon? You don't have to spend it in a boarding lounge. The airport runs free transit tours that leave straight from the terminal — a palace and Insadong in five hours, Hongdae in four, Sinpo Market in three. Most cost nothing; a couple ask for a small admission ticket at the door. Two things trip people up. First, your layover has to be 24 hours or less. Go over and you're not eligible. Second, "sold out" on the booking page isn't sold out — Incheon holds back more than half the seats for walk-ups, so turn up at the desk anyway. Terminal 1: desks 19 and 20, near Gates 1 and 2. Terminal 2: desks 5 and 6, opposite Exit 4. Be there 30 minutes early with your passport and both boarding passes. Tuesday note: Gyeongbokgung closes, so the palace tour goes to Changdeokgung instead. Staying inside? The K-Culture Zone in Terminal 1 does hanbok and Hangul name-writing in 30 minutes, free, 9 AM to 8 PM. Three decisions we need

None of these block making more content — they block posting it. Each one is a five-minute answer from someone who already knows it.

How often, starting when?

The brief is one post a week, continuously. Fifteen are ready, which is a full quarter. Pick a posting day and an order, and we keep building ahead of it rather than scrambling each week — every format here is repeatable with a new subject.

Marketing

Confirm the locations we name

The posts name hotels, Airbnbs, KTX stations and airports as places bags can be collected. Someone on product should confirm each one is currently bookable before these publish, so the copy matches what a reader actually finds.

Product

Are we cleared to state prices?

Not one post mentions a price, deliberately. If we're cleared to publish per-bag pricing and the same-day cut-off time, these posts get noticeably more persuasive.
